# Mudulakkhaṇajātaka (Ja 66)

**ID:** Ja 66
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Mudulakkhaṇajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Queen Gentle-heart
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja66
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mudulakkhaṇajātaka* (Ja 66) is a story included in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [Catalog; SuttaCentral]. Its frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana and concerns concupiscence (*saṃkilesa*): a monk residing in Sāvatthi was overcome by lust upon seeing a beautifully dressed woman, neglecting his meditation, ascetic appearance, and practice [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The canonical verse begins with the line *Ekā icchā pure āsi* [Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was an ascetic dwelling near the royal court who possessed meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and the supernormal ability to fly [Olson 2015; Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1877]. Upon arriving at the royal palace, he caught sight of Queen Mudulakkhaṇā in a disheveled state of undress, instantly fell under the sway of desire, and lost his ability to fly [Olson 2015; Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1877]. The king relinquished the queen to the lovesick ascetic, but she cured him of his infatuation by playing the role of a nagging, demanding wife [Appleton 2010]. Coming to his senses, the hermit returned the queen to the monarch, retreated to the wilderness to cultivate the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), recovered his lost *jhāna*, and attained rebirth in the Brahmaloka [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1877]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the king as Ānanda, Mudulakkhaṇā as Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ascetic as himself, leading the love-tormented monk to arahantship [Fausböll 1877].

In later Pali exegetical literature, this narrative is cited in the commentary to the fifth volume of the Jātaka collection alongside the *Lomasakassapa-*, *Hārita-*, and *Saṅkappa-jātaka*s as a cautionary example of how mindfulness lapses can cause even advanced ascetics to fall away from *jhāna* [Fausböll 1891]. Modern scholarly discussions note the tale as a narrative illustration of ascetic power and its vulnerability to sexual distraction and loss of vital mastery [Olson 2015; Appleton 2010]. SuttaCentral records an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato, and neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
